query: Which material can be used for ductility, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Using in-situ high-energy diffraction during thermomechanical processing of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy will increase its ductility by promoting beneficial dislocation processes observable in real time.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi alloy in the as-cast or homogenized condition, containing a predominantly single-phase FCC microstructure.
generation.intervention: Perform in-situ TEM or high-energy diffraction experiments while deforming the alloy to track real-time dislocation motion and phase stability; adjust processing parameters (temperature, strain rate) based on observed microstructural evolution.
generation.conditions: Testing at ambient temperature (around 25 °C), with low to moderate strain rates (e.g., 10^-3 s^-1).
generation.structural_mediator: Dynamic interactions of dislocations and/or short-range compositional fluctuations within a primarily FCC matrix, as observed via in-situ characterization.
generation.mechanism: Real-time monitoring and subsequent tuning of thermomechanical parameters will promote cross-slip and delay dislocation pile-ups in the homogeneous FCC matrix, enhancing the alloy’s capacity for plastic deformation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to conventional processing without real-time microstructural feedback, CoCrFeMnNi will show an observable increase in uniform elongation (on the order of several percent) and maintained high strength.
generation.baseline: Conventional CoCrFeMnNi, which already demonstrates notable ductility, but without in-situ guided process refinement.
generation.boundary: If processing is done at excessively high temperatures or strain rates, detrimental phase transformations or dynamic recrystallization could compromise the ductility gains.
generation.uncertainty: The precise degree of ductility enhancement remains uncertain, given that it may vary with minor compositional variations, local microstructural heterogeneities, and processing parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CoCrFeMnNi samples. For one set, monitor dislocation and phase behavior in real-time with in-situ TEM or high-energy diffraction during tension testing to adjust processing parameters. For the control set, process and test samples without real-time feedback. Compare the two sets’ elongation, yield strength, and fractography.
measurements: Tensile stress-strain curves and uniform elongation
Phase fractions and lattice parameters from diffraction patterns
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If real-time monitored samples do not achieve any measurable increase in ductility compared to unmonitored controls, the hypothesis that in-situ guided processing enhances ductility is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Unlike other conventional alloys based on a “principal element,” high-entropy alloy (HEA) is a unique material that maintains a random solid solution structure without forming intermetallic compounds in operating temperatures due to its high configurational entropy [1] – [3] . It also has outstanding physical and chemical properties, which makes it a potential replacement for traditional metallic materials, and it has recently been referred to as a multi-principal element alloy (MPEA) or compositionally concentrated alloy (CCA) [4] – [9] .

As attention in HEAs increases, many studies have been conducted to explore its mechanical, physical and chemical properties [10] – [15] . In particular, equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA, which was the first developed HEA, is the most studied because of its excellent combination of tensile strength and elongation along with excellent fracture toughness and corrosion resistance [6] , [16] – [21] . However, despite the advantages of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA, many issues arise owing to its low yield strength and costly and complex thermomechanical processing (i.e., multiple casting → hot rolling → homogenization → cold rolling → annealing → cutting, etc.

High-entropy alloys (HEAs), as a novel type of material generally consisting of five or more principle elements, have attracted extensive attention in recent years because of their attractive crystallographic and mechanical properties [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] , [7] ]. Although it is anticipated that simple solid solution phases are easier to form rather than the intermetallic compounds or complex-ordered phases due to their high configurational entropy [ [8] , [9] ], only a few HEAs have exactly single and stable solid solution structures, among which CoCrFeNiMn alloy is widely concerned [ [10] , [11] , [12] , [13] , [14] ]. It possesses a single face-center-cubic (fcc) solid solution phase even after a series of thermomechanical processing [ [15] , [16] ] and its constituent elements have more sluggish diffusion compared to other conventional alloys [ [17] ]. These characterizations contribute to excellent mechanical properties with a satisfactory combination between tensile strength and ductility [ [18] , [19] ]. decision.trend: Early work on AlCoCrFeNi-based eutectic high-entropy alloys demonstrated room-temperature ductility (PMC4145285). Subsequent studies on refractory high-entropy alloys with B2 matrices improved ductility through tailored phase transformations (PMC5995863). The equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi alloy was recognized for its stable ductility across a wide temperature range (PMC7229066); similarly, a single-phase NbTaTiV refractory alloy showed intrinsic ductility due to its edge-dislocation mobility (PMC11206460). Most recently, high-pressure–high-temperature processing of an Al0.7CoCrFeNi EHEA achieved a notable synergy of strength and ductility, highlighting the critical role of microstructure engineering (PMC11087546).
decision.unsolved: Although various high-/medium-entropy and refractory alloys exhibit noteworthy ductility, a universal strategy to optimize ductility reliably across wide ranges of composition and processing routes remains elusive. The interplay between solid-solution strengthening, precipitate control, short-range order, and microstructural stability under diverse thermomechanical conditions still requires deeper understanding and systematic study.
decision.lever: Perform in-situ TEM or high-energy diffraction experiments during deformation to track dislocation evolution, phase transformations, and microstructural refinement in real time.
decision.why: Such direct, high-resolution insights would clarify the active ductility-enhancing mechanisms in these complex alloys, illuminate optimal processing routes, and guide the selection of suitable compositions and phases to maximize plastic deformation capacity.
